1:
Who the man with the measuring line is gets four answers. Calvin makes him an angel appearing in human form, and says why such a being is called a man at all: angels put on that form only for a time and are so named without strict propriety, God treating us as children and giving them easier access; if it be asked whether they really took human nature, they never truly became men. Henry identifies him with Christ, the master builder of his church, who builds exactly by line and level. Clarke thinks him a representation of the cup-bearer who afterwards had commission to build the walls, the city having until then remained unenclosed. Ellicott denies that he is an angel at all, since he has no message and no mission, and calls him a mere figure in the vision, implicitly rebuked for what he is doing.

Who the young man is divides them again. Keil and Delitzsch argue that it must be the prophet, since the answer is not what the measurer needed — he could satisfy himself by measuring — but an announcement to carry to the people; and they refuse the suggestion that the title slights his inexperience, since no man could know the city's future without a revelation. Henry agrees and turns the youth into an argument, that the prophet entered on his office young and no man ought to despise that, though such a one might fear the worst and must be bidden to hope the best. Ellicott takes the other side: it gives a much more definite turn to the vision to refer the words to the man who was measuring, and he calls it a forcing of them to make the title turn on ignorance.

On the errand of the second angel two of them differ. Ellicott insists that the speaker is that angel and not the interpreter, since otherwise the figure would be superfluous, the interpreter being able to address the young man directly. Henry has the interpreter going forth as he designed and the other meeting him to ask that the vision be explained first; Wesley identifies that interpreter with Christ.

The measuring itself all take as promise rather than threat. Gill notes that a Jewish commentator allows the vision to refer to the days of the Messiah, granting it might also encourage those then present about a literal rebuilding. Henry distinguishes this line from the line of confusion and from the line stretched out for destruction, and reads the city as one lost in its own suburbs, extended as freely as if it had no walls and yet as safe as if it had the strongest. Clarke cites a historian for the fulfilment, that the city overflowing with inhabitants extended beyond its walls; Ellicott cites the same passage more exactly, naming the hill taken in and fortified. Wesley reads the promise of the suburbs as covering extent and safety alike.

The wall of fire is glossed by all and pressed furthest by one. Clarke states it plainly, that her safety consists in the divine defence and no adversary may touch her, though much must refer to a city yet to come. Ellicott guards the promise from being made an argument against building, since walls were built not long after, and treats the troubles between as chastisements not proportioned to the transgressions. Wesley reduces the second half of the verse to a sentence: the divine presence and favour make her glorious. Gill and Henry both trace the figure to the fires travellers and shepherds kindled about their camps to keep off beasts of prey, and Gill pursues the natural history for its own sake, gathering from an ancient writer and two modern travellers that lions fear fire above all things, yet will sometimes outbrave it and leap into the fold to drag away a sheep.
6:
Henry alone explains why a second summons was needed. The proclamation of Cyrus might have brought them all back, yet only some forty thousand went; the land of their captivity was to most of them the land of their birth, where they had taken root and some had got estates, and they thought they could not better themselves by going back. He traces it to distrust of the promise and love of ease, and notes the harm to those who had gone, staying behind censuring them as rash and weakening their hands. Wesley calls the doubled cry an address to sleepy men; Gill notes that the repetition confirms the call, as a Jewish commentator observes; Clarke and Ellicott alike make the land of the north Babylonia and the regions round it.

The clause about spreading abroad admits two tenses, and Ellicott sets them out. Taken as a past, it means scattered and refers to dispersions already made, the exiles being settled by then over a hundred provinces and more; taken as a prophetic perfect, it means God has fixed his intention to spread them abroad, the flight being urged both by the judgments about to fall on the city and by the blessing intended. He rejects a third rendering, that God will scatter them to the four winds in some new dispersion, as resting on a linguistic error, and notes that the ancient Greek paraphrased the other way, gathering them from the four winds rather than scattering them to it. Wesley states the same balance without the grammar: as the threat was executed in scattering them, so the promise will be performed in gathering them; Henry adds that since God owns the scattering to have been in wrath, the invitation is a token of willingness to be reconciled.

Why Zion should be told to deliver herself is answered by two. Ellicott takes the daughter of Babylon for that city's inhabitants, as the daughter of Zion means Zion's. Henry explains the odd phrase that Zion dwells there at all: many of her sons dwelt in that city, and where the people of God are the church of God is, not being tied to places; but she is in danger of partaking both in that city's sins and in her plagues.

The phrase rendered after the glory is the crux of the passage and gets two treatments. Clarke prints a correspondent's argument that the words are unintelligible as they stand and should be rendered the future glory, which would make the passage a prophecy of the Messiah; the person speaking is distinguished from the Lord of hosts as sent by him and yet is himself called by the divine name, and the lawgiver who asked to see that glory was shown only what came after. Ellicott takes the words to mean in search of glory, to display it upon the heathen by first breaking their power and afterwards attaching them to his service. Gill reaches the same conclusion by a shorter road, taking the speaker for Christ, the true Jehovah, as his being sent shows.

Two further notes stand out. On the apple of the eye Clarke observes that anyone looking into another's eye sees his own image in miniature in the pupil, wonders whether an English word for an infant comes from the Hebrew term, and draws that the follower of God is ever impressed on the eye of God. On the shaking of the hand Gill says the destruction needs no more than that bare gesture, and Clarke has the threat first and the stroke after. Ellicott supplies documentary evidence, a great rock inscription cut by Darius recording two insurrections in Babylonia and the taking of the city twice, by the king himself and by his general. Keil and Delitzsch render the verses through and carry straight on into the summons to rejoice.
10:
Henry sets the summons to sing against the circumstances of those who first heard it. The returned Jews were in distress, their neighbours spiteful and their brethren in Babylon cool and unwilling to assist them; yet they are told to rejoice, since those who have recovered purity and liberty may sing before they recover prosperity. Gill follows the Targum in reading the daughter of Zion as the congregation of Zion.

The promise to dwell in the midst of them is given a double fulfilment, and they weight the halves differently. Henry says it is repeated because it was to have two accomplishments, the first in the temple worship and the second in the incarnation, the speaker being himself sent by the Lord of hosts and so the Lord who dwelt among them. Ellicott agrees that the prophet meant it first of the second temple, but adds that the visible manifestation was never given there again, and calls the later fulfilment one little dreamt of by him. Clarke tips the balance the other way, referring it chiefly to the Christian church, in which God dwells by his Spirit as he had once by a symbol; Wesley divides it evenly, fulfilled in part to the Jews and more fully to the gospel church.

On the many nations joined to the Lord, Clarke and Henry contradict each other about the past. Clarke says roundly that no nation ever became converts to the Jewish religion, whereas whole nations have embraced the faith of Christ, so the verse belongs to the Christian church alone. Henry holds that the nation multiplied greatly by proselytes after the captivity, naturalized and entitled to all the privileges of native Israelites, and reads that as an earnest of the calling of the Gentiles; he remarks how strange it is that what was promised as a blessing in the prophets' time should have been so great an offence in the apostles'.

Ellicott collects the variants of the ancient Greek there. Where the received text has the nations joined to the Lord, the old version has them fleeing to him for refuge; where it has I will dwell, they shall dwell. He notes that the closing words about the sending imply a fulfilment near enough to prove the speaker's commission, and ends with the irony that when the promise was fulfilled it was precisely the city that failed to perceive it.

What the Lord inherits is defined narrowly by two and broadly by others. Keil and Delitzsch ground the phrase on the older passage where the nation is called the Lord's portion, and take the name here for the delivered remnant, gathered out of Babel to dwell on holy ground. Ellicott observes that this is the only place where the term the holy land occurs, and makes an admission none of the others does: the promise has not been literally fulfilled, the coming of Christ having been the beginning of the rejection of that people and the destruction of their city. He does not treat the discrepancy as damaging, the prophets having seen only as in a mirror and no one of them receiving the truth entire. Gill expects a return of the believing Jews to that land, Clarke a final restoration, and Wesley glosses the verb as to claim, recover and delight in, as a man does in a paternal inheritance.

The command to be silent is read as awe by all who touch it. Gill takes it for astonishment at the work, so that none dare open his mouth against it, and reports that the Targum turns the words on the wicked. Clarke has the nations amazed as God arises to deliver an ancient people; Wesley makes it reverence and expectation at once, God being already at the work and not sitting down again until it is done; Keil and Delitzsch render the verse and leave it.
